posts.title: Decide the care home move after recovery has had its chance
posts.insight: Recovery after a broken hip goes on for months, with leg function reaching its best close to a year later on average in one large study. A permanent care home decision made in the first weeks is made while recovery has only just started.
posts.angle: Owns the collection's argument about timing: where it is safe, do not decide a permanent care home move while recovery has only just started. A care home can be the right choice; the question is when to decide and who is at the centre of the decision.
posts.position_basis: mixed: recovery times, rehabilitation effect and policy summary are empirical or documented (Magaziner 2000, Dyer 2016, Cochrane 2021, Harrison 2017); 'wait for rehabilitation before deciding, where safe' is ethical and clinical judgement, marked as such

captions.x:
After a broken hip, leg function can keep improving for close to a year. In one large US study of people who lived at home before the fracture (1990 to 1991), that was how long it took on average to reach its best.

Across many studies, most of the recovery in walking and daily activities came in the first 6 months. Roughly 4 to 6 in 10 people got back to the mobility they had before.

Recovery goes on for months, so in the first weeks in hospital a person is usually well short of where they will get to. In our view, that is the wrong moment to settle a permanent move to a care home, unless there is no safe alternative.

A 2017 paper summarised policy in England and Scotland as saying that moving into a care home straight from an acute ward should be avoided where possible.

Sometimes a care home is the right choice. You should be at the centre of it, and it should rest on how you are after rehabilitation.

Ask: what rehabilitation is planned, and when will we look at this again?
captions.linkedin:
After a broken hip, leg function can keep improving for close to a year. In one large US study of people who lived at home before the fracture, that was the average time for leg function to reach its best. Mood, arm function and thinking reached their best at about 4 months.

A later review of many studies found that most of the recovery in walking and daily activities came in the first 6 months. Roughly 4 to 6 in 10 people got back to the mobility they had before the fracture. Fewer people who came from care homes did so.

These are averages. Reaching your best is not the same as a full recovery, and some people never regain their earlier function.

Rehabilitation may change the picture. In trials, rehabilitation in hospital led by a specialist team probably meant fewer people died or needed a move to a care home over the next 6 to 12 months: about 31 in 100, compared with 35 in 100 on an illustrative usual-care risk. That figure combines deaths and moves to more care.

A 2017 paper summarised policy in England and Scotland as saying that moving into a care home straight from an acute hospital ward should be avoided where possible.

Our judgement: recovery goes on for months, so in the first weeks after a hip fracture a person is usually well short of where they will get to. Where it is safe, a permanent care home decision should wait until the person has had time and rehabilitation to recover. Sometimes a care home is the right choice. The person should be at the centre of that decision either way.

Questions you or your family can ask:
1. What rehabilitation is planned, and for how long?
2. When will we look at this decision again?
3. What would need to change for going home to be possible?

Sources: Magaziner et al, J Gerontol 2000; Dyer et al, BMC Geriatr 2016; Handoll et al, Cochrane 2021; Harrison et al, Age Ageing 2017.

posts.title: Block the pain before the moving
posts.insight: Pain from a broken hip is mostly on movement. A nerve block in the emergency department reduced pain on movement within half an hour compared with no block, and lasts several hours, which can cover the X-ray, the move to the ward and early nursing care.
posts.angle: Time the block early, in the emergency department, before the moves rather than after them; families can ask whether one has been offered. The block does not last until surgery, which is why guidance advises another at the time of the operation.
posts.position_basis: mixed: effect sizes and guidance are empirical or documented (Cochrane 2020, Association of Anaesthetists 2020, Scottish standards, NICE); 'give it early, before the moves' is clinical interpretation consistent with the Scottish and anaesthetic guidance

captions.x:
Pain from a broken hip is often mild while lying still and severe when the person is moved. Scotland's hip fracture standards say so, and name a nerve block as the first choice for pain relief in the emergency department.

A nerve block is an injection of local anaesthetic near the nerves to the hip. A Cochrane review found it reduced pain on movement within half an hour by about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale, compared with no block.

One injection gives several hours of relief, not relief until the operation. Given early in the emergency department, it can cover the X-ray, the move to the ward and the first hours of nursing care, for as long as it lasts. UK anaesthetic guidance advises another block at surgery.

If someone you love has broken a hip, ask: has a nerve block been offered?
captions.linkedin:
Pain from a broken hip is often mild while the person lies still and severe when they are moved. Scotland's national hip fracture standards make this point, and name a fascia iliaca block as the first choice for pain relief in the emergency department.

A nerve block is an injection of local anaesthetic near the nerves that supply the hip.

What the evidence shows:
1. A Cochrane review found that a block reduced pain on movement within half an hour by about 2.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale, compared with no block. This result comes from 11 trials with 503 people, and everyone could have other pain relief too.
2. Blocks probably mean fewer chest infections and getting out of bed about 11 hours sooner, though these results come from only a few small trials.
3. People with dementia were often left out of these trials.

Timing is the practical detail. A single injection gives several hours of relief: about 8 hours with a long-acting local anaesthetic in one review, while trials measured benefit only to 4 hours. Given early in the emergency department, it can cover the X-ray, the move to the ward and the first hours of nursing care, for as long as it lasts. The Association of Anaesthetists also advises another block at the time of surgery.

NICE asks for pain relief good enough to allow moving for X-rays, nursing care and rehabilitation, and says a block should be considered when paracetamol and morphine-type drugs are not enough.

Staff can time the block before the moves rather than after them. Families can ask whether one has been offered.

posts.title: Fast enough, and faster
posts.insight: HIP ATTACK found that surgery within about 6 hours did not clearly reduce deaths or major complications compared with a median of 24 hours, while observational data link waits beyond a day with slightly more deaths. The two answer different questions.
posts.angle: The target is removing avoidable delay (day of or day after admission, within 36 hours), not racing to operate within hours. Both findings can be true.
posts.position_basis: mixed: trial and cohort results are empirical; reconciling them into 'remove avoidable delay' is clinical interpretation consistent with UK guidance

captions.x:
HIP ATTACK randomised 2,970 people with hip fracture in 17 countries to surgery at a median of 6 hours or 24 hours after diagnosis.

At 90 days, 9 in 100 had died in the fast group and 10 in 100 with usual care. Death or a major complication (a combined measure): 22 in 100 in both. Accelerated surgery did not clearly reduce either, though a small benefit is not ruled out.

In secondary outcomes, as summarised in UK anaesthetic guidance, the fast group got up sooner and left hospital sooner, with no sign of harm.

In Ontario, waits over 24 hours were linked with slightly more deaths at 30 days: 6.5 vs 5.8 in 100. That is an association.

These answer different questions: very fast against fairly fast, and avoidable delay beyond a day. NICE asks for surgery on the day of admission or the day after. UK anaesthetic guidance and the Scottish standard say within 36 hours. Remove the avoidable delay.

More posts in the Reading the evidence series put trials and observational studies side by side.
captions.linkedin:
HIP ATTACK randomised 2,970 people with hip fracture, in 69 hospitals across 17 countries, to accelerated surgery or usual care. Median time from diagnosis to surgery was 6 hours and 24 hours.

At 90 days, about 9 in 100 had died in the accelerated group and 10 in 100 in the usual-care group. Death or a major complication (a combined measure) affected about 22 in 100 in both. Accelerated surgery did not clearly reduce either outcome. The uncertainty range runs from about 1 more to 3 fewer deaths per 100, so a small benefit is possible.

Secondary outcomes favoured speed: the accelerated group got up and about sooner and left hospital sooner, with no sign of harm (as summarised in the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 guideline).

Note what the comparison was. Half of the usual-care group had surgery within about 24 hours of diagnosis, and three quarters within about 42 hours. The trial tested very fast against fairly fast.

Observational data ask a different question. In more than 40,000 people in Ontario, those who waited more than 24 hours from arrival were slightly more likely to die within 30 days: about 6.5 in 100 compared with 5.8 in 100 in matched people operated on sooner. That is a link; people who wait may be sicker.

UK guidance asks for surgery on the day of admission or the day after (NICE) and within 36 hours (Association of Anaesthetists; Scottish standard).

Our reading: the target is removing avoidable delay, rather than operating as fast as is physically possible. The trial did not show that racing saves lives, though the fast group got up and left hospital sooner; the cohort data do not excuse drift beyond a day or two.

More posts in the Reading the evidence series put trials and observational studies side by side.

posts.title: Care without an operation, for a very small group
posts.insight: NICE's guideline group describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip. For a very small group of very frail people near the end of life, a Dutch study of people who chose care without an operation, after discussion, found quality of life rated a little lower by relatives in the following weeks, within a margin set in advance; pain relief without surgery has to be good.
posts.angle: Care without an operation is active care, not doing nothing; it deserves open discussion for the few for whom surgery is unlikely to add good time, and it is no default for anyone because they are old or frail.
posts.position_basis: mixed: FRAIL-HIP findings and guidance are empirical or documented; that non-operative care should be discussable and never a default by age is ethical judgement, marked as such

captions.x:
NICE's guideline group describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip, and says surgery should still be considered when a hip fracture comes with a terminal illness.

A Dutch study looked at a very different group: 172 very frail care home residents, median age 88, with short life expectancy. After discussion, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose surgery. They chose; nobody was randomised.

Relatives and staff rated quality of life in the following weeks. Scores were a little lower without an operation, but within a margin the researchers set in advance. About 8 in 10 of those who chose no operation died within a month, against 1 in 4 after surgery. The frailest people chose no operation, so that gap does not show the effect of surgery.

The researchers judged pain undertreated without surgery, and 2 people switched to an operation as their pain grew worse.

We should be able to talk about care without an operation for this small group, with strong pain relief. It should never be a default because someone is old.
captions.linkedin:
NICE's guideline group describes surgery as the best form of pain relief for a broken hip, and says that even when a hip fracture comes with a terminal illness, the team should still consider surgery as part of palliative care (care that eases pain and respects the person's wishes).

A Dutch study, FRAIL-HIP, looked at a very different group from most people with a broken hip. It followed 172 very frail care home residents, median age 88, whose life expectancy was already short. After talking it through, 88 chose care without an operation and 84 chose an operation. People chose; they were not allocated at random.

What it found:
1. Relatives and care staff rated quality of life in the following weeks. Scores were a little lower when there was no operation, but within a margin the researchers set in advance. These were other people's ratings, and comparisons after about a month are unreliable because most of the non-operative group had died.
2. About 8 in 10 of those who chose no operation died within a month, compared with 1 in 4 of those who had surgery. The frailest people chose no operation, so this gap does not show what the operation itself did.
3. Among relatives who answered about a death without an operation, about half rated the dying as good to almost perfect.
4. The researchers judged that pain was undertreated without an operation, and 2 people changed to surgery because their pain grew worse.

Scotland's hip fracture standards expect a written care or palliative care plan if a decision not to operate is agreed, and a fresh look at the decision if the person gets better.

Our judgement: care without an operation is active care. It needs regular, strong pain relief, careful nursing and support for the family. For a very small group it deserves an open conversation. It should never be offered as a default because someone is old, frail or has dementia.
captions.bluesky:
NICE's guideline group calls surgery the best pain relief for a broken hip.

In a Dutch study of 172 very frail care home residents, those who chose no operation had quality of life rated a little lower, within a preset margin. About 8 in 10 died within a month. Researchers judged pain undertreated.
captions.threads:
NICE's guideline group calls surgery the best pain relief for a broken hip.

A Dutch study followed 172 very frail care home residents with short life expectancy who chose whether to have surgery. Of those who chose none, about 8 in 10 died within a month. Relatives rated quality of life a little lower, within a preset margin. Researchers judged pain undertreated.

We should be able to discuss care without an operation for a few people, with strong pain relief. Never as a default for age.

posts.title: Partial weight-bearing: none of 16 older people kept to it throughout
posts.insight: In an insole-sensor study, none of 16 older people kept to a partial weight-bearing limit throughout after hip fracture surgery, and restriction in a second study reduced mobility without reducing load. NICE says to operate so the person can bear full weight straight away.
posts.angle: Restricted weight-bearing after hip fracture surgery in older adults mostly buys less walking, not less load. Any restriction should come with a reason and a plan for how the person will move.
posts.position_basis: mixed: compliance and mobility findings are empirical (small studies); NICE aim is documented; harm evidence stated as mixed; the closing question is clinical judgement

captions.x:
Sixteen older people (aged 75 and over) walked on pressure-sensing insoles after hip fracture surgery, told to put only part of their weight through the leg.

None kept to the limit throughout; one managed it briefly. 11 of the 16 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. 14 of 18 young adults with ankle fractures kept to almost all of it.

In a second small study from the same group, older people told to restrict weight walked more slowly and had lower mobility scores on day 5, yet pressed just as hard through the leg.

NICE says to operate with the aim of full, unrestricted weight-bearing straight after surgery.

If a restriction is written, ask: what is the reason, and how will this person move safely meanwhile?
captions.linkedin:
Sixteen older people (aged 75 and over) walked on pressure-sensing insoles after hip fracture surgery, each told to put only part of their weight through the operated leg.

None kept to the limit throughout the walk; one managed it briefly. 11 of the 16 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. By contrast, 14 of 18 young adults with ankle fractures kept to almost the entire restriction. (Kammerlander et al, J Bone Joint Surg Am 2018; one walking session, one centre.)

A second small German study, from the same research group, compared older people told to limit weight with those allowed full weight. The restricted group walked more slowly and had lower mobility scores on day 5, but pressed just as hard through the leg. It was a before-and-after comparison, not a randomised trial.

In these two small studies, older people told to restrict weight walked more slowly but did not load the leg any less.

NICE guidance says surgeons should operate with the aim of letting the person bear full weight, without restriction, straight after surgery. That is an aim, not a ban: clinicians still restrict weight-bearing for some fractures and fixations.

A question for the physiotherapist or the ward round: what is the reason for this restriction, and how will this person move safely in the meantime?
captions.bluesky:
With pressure-sensing insoles, none of 16 people aged 75 and over kept to a partial weight-bearing limit throughout after hip fracture surgery; 11 put over twice the permitted weight through the leg.

NICE: operate so people can bear full weight straight away. If restricted, ask why.
captions.threads:
In a German insole study, none of 16 older people kept to a partial weight-bearing limit throughout after hip fracture surgery; 11 put more than twice the permitted weight through the leg. A second small, non-randomised study found that people told to restrict weight walked more slowly but loaded the leg just as much.

NICE says to operate aiming for full weight-bearing straight away.

If a restriction is written, ask for the reason and the plan for moving safely.

posts.title: Treat now so surgery is not delayed
posts.insight: NICE frames nine correctable problems as things to find and treat straight away so they do not delay hip fracture surgery; routine tests that will not change the operation, waiting for an echocardiogram, and aspirin or clopidogrel are not reasons to wait.
posts.angle: Use NICE's own framing: the list is a to-do list for the first hours, not a list of reasons to postpone. Any hold-up should name the problem and the time by which it will be corrected (marked as judgement).
posts.position_basis: mixed: the NICE list, echo and antiplatelet advice, and the 36-hour statement are documented guidance; 'name the problem and a time' is ethical and clinical judgement

captions.x:
NICE lists nine problems to find and treat straight away, so that they do not delay hip fracture surgery: anaemia, anticoagulation, dehydration, electrolyte problems, uncontrolled diabetes, uncontrolled heart failure, a correctable arrhythmia or ischaemia, chest infection, and a flare of chronic lung disease.

That is a to-do list for the first hours.

NICE's guideline developers wrote that people should not wait for routine tests that will not change the operation or anaesthetic. UK anaesthetic guidance says not to wait for an echocardiogram, and since 2011 not to delay for aspirin or clopidogrel.

UK guidance says 36 hours is enough time to correct the medical obstacles to surgery if work starts at once.

We should expect any delay to name the problem and the time it will be fixed.
captions.linkedin:
NICE lists nine problems to find and treat straight away, so that they do not delay hip fracture surgery:
1. Anaemia
2. Anticoagulation
3. Volume depletion (dehydration)
4. Electrolyte imbalance
5. Uncontrolled diabetes
6. Uncontrolled heart failure
7. Correctable cardiac arrhythmia or ischaemia
8. Acute chest infection
9. Exacerbation of a chronic chest condition

NICE frames these as problems to correct immediately. It is a to-do list for the first hours, rather than a list of reasons to postpone.

Three things that should not hold up the operation:

Routine tests that will not change the operation or the anaesthetic. NICE's guideline developers wrote that people should not be kept waiting for them.

An echocardiogram. The Association of Anaesthetists says not to delay surgery for one: the result rarely changes how the anaesthetic is given, and a valve problem is very unlikely to be treated before the hip. It still expects careful, monitored anaesthesia.

Aspirin or clopidogrel. Association of Anaesthetists guidance has advised since 2011, restated in its 2020 update, that surgery should not be delayed for these. Observational studies of people on clopidogrel having early surgery found slightly more transfusions but no rise in deaths. Warfarin is an anticoagulant, needs reversal, and belongs on the NICE list.

The 2020 guidance says 36 hours (or less) is enough time to correct medical obstacles to surgery, and that the team should say what needs to happen and document any decisions. The Scottish standards add that surgery should not be delayed unless the benefits of more medical treatment outweigh the risks of waiting, and that 36 hours is enough if the work starts at once.

Our view: when a delay is given a medical reason, the record should name the problem being corrected and the time by which it will be corrected.

posts.title: A normal X-ray, and still can't stand
posts.insight: X-rays find most broken hips, but if a fracture is still suspected after normal X-rays, NICE says to offer an MRI (or consider CT if MRI is not available within 24 hours). Not being able to take weight on the leg the next day, despite pain relief, is a reason to look again.
posts.angle: Give families and care workers the question that should outlast a normal X-ray: can the person take weight on that leg? If not, ask whether an MRI is needed.
posts.position_basis: mixed: NICE recommendation and guideline text and the Haj-Mirzaian review are documented or empirical; prompting families to ask is practical judgement

captions.x:
A hip X-ray finds most broken hips, but not all. The NICE guideline estimates X-rays find 90 to 98 in every 100 broken hips.

But if the person still can't take weight on the leg the day after the injury, despite good pain relief, the guideline says doctors should look again and strongly suspect a hip fracture. If one is still suspected after normal X-rays, NICE says to offer an MRI, or consider a CT scan if MRI isn't available within 24 hours.

In a pooled review of studies of older people whose X-rays showed no definite fracture but whose doctors still suspected one, MRI found a hip fracture needing surgery in about 4 in 10.

If you are a relative or care worker, you can ask: "They still can't take weight on that leg. Could the X-ray have missed a fracture? Is an MRI needed?"
captions.linkedin:
A hip X-ray finds most broken hips, but not all. It is not the end of the question if the person still can't take weight on the leg the next day.

The NICE guideline estimates that X-rays pick up 90 to 98 in every 100 broken hips.

Being unable to take weight on the leg is a typical sign of a broken hip. The NICE guideline says that if someone still can't take weight on the leg the day after the injury, despite good pain relief, doctors should look again and strongly suspect a hip fracture. Being able to stand does not rule one out, and not being able to stand can have other causes, such as bruising.

If a broken hip is still suspected after normal hip X-rays, NICE says to offer an MRI scan. If MRI isn't available within 24 hours, or can't be done, it says to consider a CT scan. (NICE guidance applies formally to England and Wales.)

How often is something found? A review of 35 studies looked at older people (average age 77) whose doctors suspected a hip fracture that the X-ray did not show. In the studies of people whose X-rays showed no definite fracture, MRI found a hip fracture of a type needing surgery in about 4 in 10. That figure applies to this selected group, not to everyone with hip pain after a fall.

If you are a relative or a care worker, the words to use are: "They still can't take weight on that leg. Could there be a hip fracture the X-ray didn't show? Is an MRI needed?"

posts.title: Who signs the form?
posts.insight: In England and Wales, being next of kin does not give you legal power to consent to an operation for an adult who can't decide. An appointed health and welfare attorney or court deputy may; otherwise the doctor decides in the person's best interests. In Scotland a doctor completes a certificate of incapacity and seeks a welfare attorney's consent where reasonable and practicable. In both, the person's wishes must be taken into account.
posts.angle: The family's usual legal role is to inform the decision, not make it; the most useful thing they bring is what the person would want. Families should be told who is deciding and on what basis (judgement).
posts.position_basis: mixed: the legal position is documented in peer-reviewed summaries (Wade 2019, Orr 2018, Edwardson 2018, Zalmay 2021); being told who decides and why is ethical judgement

captions.x:
In England and Wales, being next of kin does not give you the legal right to consent to an operation for your mother.

If she can't decide for herself, the decision falls to someone she appointed under a registered lasting power of attorney for health and welfare, or to a court-appointed deputy with that power (unless a valid advance decision applies). If there is no one like that, the doctor responsible usually decides, in her best interests. Her wishes, values and beliefs must be taken into account, and family or close friends should be consulted if there is time.

In Scotland the law is different. A doctor completes a certificate of incapacity. If she appointed a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must seek that attorney's consent where reasonable and practicable. Her past and present wishes must be taken into account as far as practicable.

You can ask: who is making this decision, and on what basis?
captions.linkedin:
In England and Wales, being next of kin does not give you the legal right to consent to an operation for your mother. Hip fracture surgery is usually needed quickly, and some people can't decide for themselves at that moment.

In England and Wales (Mental Capacity Act 2005), if she can't decide, the decision is made by:
1. Someone she appointed under a lasting power of attorney for health and welfare, which must be registered to be used, or
2. A court-appointed deputy with that power, or
3. If there is no one like that, usually the doctor responsible, in her best interests.

The decision must take account of what she would want: her wishes, values and beliefs. Family or close friends should be consulted if there is time. In an emergency that conversation may be brief.

In Scotland the law is different. A doctor completes a certificate of incapacity, which allows treatment. If she has appointed a welfare attorney with power over medical decisions, the doctor must ask for that attorney's consent where it is reasonable and practicable. Her past and present wishes and feelings must be taken into account, and certain people must be consulted.

Capacity is about one decision at one time. A person may be able to make some decisions but not others, and it can change during the day. You can ask whether she could decide with help, or later in the day, though a hip operation can't wait long.

Our view: you should be told clearly who is making the decision and on what legal basis, and asked what she would want.

Questions you can ask:
Who is making this decision?
Could she decide for herself, with help or at another time?
What do you need to know about what she would want?

posts.title: Watch the first drink after surgery
posts.insight: Roughly 1 in 3 older people have trouble swallowing after hip fracture surgery, and many don't notice it themselves. Watching the first drinks and meals, sitting fully upright, for coughing, a changed voice or repeated swallows gives a reason to ask for a swallowing assessment.
posts.angle: Swallowing problems are thought of as a stroke problem; after hip fracture they are common and easy to miss. The first drink after surgery is a moment when staff and family are both present.
posts.position_basis: mixed: prevalence, associations and warning signs are empirical or consensus (Love 2013, Suzuki 2023, Mateos-Nozal 2021, Allen 2020, ESSD-EUGMS 2016); watching the first drink is clinical judgement, not a tested intervention

captions.x:
The first drink after a hip operation is a good moment to watch the swallow.

In one Australian unit, about 1 in 3 older people (61 of 181) had trouble swallowing after hip fracture surgery. It was more common in people who were older, came from a care home, or had a neurological or lung condition.

Signs to watch for: coughing or choking, a hoarse or changed voice after swallowing, lots of throat clearing, several swallows for one mouthful, food left in the mouth. Many older people don't notice these themselves.

Sit fully upright to eat and drink, and stay upright for at least half an hour after a meal.

If you see these signs, ask the ward for a swallowing assessment.
captions.linkedin:
The first drink after a hip operation is a good moment to watch the swallow.

In one Australian hospital unit, about 1 in 3 older people (61 of 181) had trouble swallowing after hip fracture surgery. Across studies the average is roughly a third, with wide variation; one Spanish study that tested everyone with a bedside test found more than half.

Trouble swallowing was more common in people who were older, came from a care home, or already had a neurological or lung condition.

In a New Zealand hospital, people with hip fracture and a recorded swallowing problem had aspiration pneumonia (a chest infection from food or drink going the wrong way) far more often: about 1 in 10, compared with fewer than 1 in 100. They were also more likely to die within 30 days. They were older on average, and this link does not show that the swallowing problem caused the deaths. We did not find a study showing that watching the first drink prevents pneumonia.

Signs to watch for at a drink or meal, from a European consensus paper:
1. Coughing or choking
2. A hoarse or changed voice after swallowing
3. Lots of throat clearing
4. Swallowing several times for one mouthful
5. Food left in the mouth

Many older people don't notice these problems themselves. Sitting fully upright to eat and drink, and staying upright for at least half an hour after a meal, is standard advice. After hip surgery that may need help and good pain relief.

Families may be present at the first drink as well as staff. If you see these signs, ask for a swallowing assessment.

posts.follow_note: Small, practical ward details with the evidence behind them.
posts.verification_notes: Love 2013 (abstract): 61 of 181 (C03-07-a) and associations (C03-07-c; delirium association omitted, excluded topic). Suzuki 2023 and Mateos-Nozal 2021 (abstracts): roughly a third on average, over half with bedside testing (C03-07-b). Allen 2020 (abstract): unadjusted association with aspiration pneumonia and 30-day death, older group (C03-07-d); 18 vs 4 in 100 not repeated in X. ESSD-EUGMS 2016 (full text): signs and upright posture (C03-07-e/f), source wording 'hoarse or changed voice'. The ask for an assessment is advice (C03-07-g not found: no staff group named). No claim that watching prevents pneumonia.
open_issues: Checker flag 'Aging' (us_spelling?) in the visual credit line is the journal title Clin Interv Aging; kept as a proper name.
